hook.text: Cross two inbred corn lines and the offspring outperforms both parents. Farmers call it hybrid vigor.

buildup.text: Inbreeding weakens plants over generations. But crossing two inbred lines produces an explosive burst of growth.

discovery.text: Hybrid corn yields jumped 20–30% over open-pollinated varieties. The US adopted hybrids almost completely by 1960.

twist.text: Farmers can't save hybrid seeds—offspring lose vigor. They must buy new seed every year from companies.

climax.text: This dependence on purchased seed industrialized agriculture and reshaped the seed business forever.

punchline.text: Better seeds, but only if you buy them every season.

quiz.question: Why can't farmers save and replant hybrid seeds?
options: Offspring lose hybrid vigor and underperform

details.summary: Hybrid vigor (heterosis) is the phenomenon where crossing two genetically distinct parent lines produces offspring with superior growth, yield, and resilience. This principle revolutionized corn production in the 1930s and later transformed rice and other crops in the Green Revolution.
details.whyItMatters: Hybrid vigor has increased crop yields by 15-50% across major cereals. Hybrid corn, rice, and sorghum now feed billions of people, though the requirement to purchase new seed each year has transformed the economics of farming.
takeaways: Hybrid vigor produces offspring 15-50% more productive than either parent line
U.S. hybrid corn in the 1930s was the first major commercial application of heterosis
Hybrid rice developed by Yuan Longping feeds billions across Asia today

faq.question: What causes hybrid vigor in crop plants?
faq.answer: When two genetically different inbred lines are crossed, the offspring inherit complementary genes from both parents. Harmful recessive genes from one parent are masked by dominant genes from the other. The result is plants that are more vigorous, productive, and stress-tolerant than either parent.

faq.question: Why must farmers buy new hybrid seed every year?
faq.answer: Hybrid vigor only occurs in the first generation (F1). Seeds saved from hybrid plants segregate into variable offspring that lose the yield advantage. Farmers must purchase fresh F1 seed annually, which increases costs but also guarantees consistent high performance.
